Fig. 02Architectural Specification
Axum 0.8 · Tokio 1.40 · Matchit Radix

Designed fordeterministic speed.

Axum and Hyper handle the raw socket. A proc-macro turns your RSX into straight-line contiguous buffer writes. The result is a single native binary with zero interpreter, zero virtual DOM and zero garbage collector between the request and the response.

Traditional SSR frameworks load an entire JavaScript runtime, parse trees dynamically on the heap, and run garbage collection passes during peak load. Yav computes template topology at compile-time and streams bytes directly into kernel socket buffers.

2.1Execution pipeline280 µs socket-to-wire

From socket to wire in 280 microseconds.

Every incoming HTTP request traverses five zero-allocation, compile-time specialized phases. There are no virtual DOM trees, no intermediate JavaScript bridges, and zero memory allocations on the hot path.

Stage 01 — Socket Ingress & Frame Parsing~38 µs
Heap Allocation: 0 B heap (Zero-Copy)
Kernel Syscall: epoll_wait / accept4
Concurrency: Tokio Work-Stealing

Non-blocking Tokio worker accepts TCP/TLS socket; Hyper parses HTTP frames directly into unallocated slices.

2.2Memory Architecturezero VDOM heap overhead

Compile-time layout vs runtime VDOM.

Traditional web frameworks allocate a dynamic Virtual DOM tree on every single render. Hundreds of micro-objects are scattered across the heap, followed by expensive tree-diffing algorithms and periodic garbage collector pauses.

Yav moves this entire topology analysis to <strong class="text-paper font-semibold">compile time</strong>. The Rust compiler embeds all static HTML fragments directly into the read-only data segment (<code class="text-oxide font-mono">.rodata</code>) of the binary. At runtime, dynamic components merely append slices into a single contiguous buffer.

Why Contiguous Memory Wins

A single pre-sized buffer stays inside L1/L2 CPU cache lines (64 bytes). Pointer-chasing tree structures trigger constant RAM cache misses.

MEMORY TOPOLOGY COMPARISONHeap Allocation Analysis
Traditional VDOM (Next.js / Nuxt / Leptos WASM)~350–500 KB heap allocations / req
Heap: [VNode*] -> [Props HashMap] -> [Children Vec] -> [Diff Tree]Cache Misses
Yav Proc-Macro Compiled Slices0 dynamic allocations (L1 cache)
.rodata: [&'static str (headers)] + [&'static str (footers)] -> BytesMutZero-Copy
MACRO EXPANSION UNDER THE HOOD

rsx! { <div class="card"><h2>{title}</h2></div> }

// 2. What the compiler emits into machine code:

2.3Crate compositionmodular architecture

Small crates. Hard edges.

Yav is intentionally decomposed into focused crates with strict boundaries and zero circular dependencies. Each crate can be audited, imported or replaced independently.

2.4Security Architecturezero external state

Cryptographic sessions. Zero Redis dependency.

Traditional frameworks query a Redis cluster or database on every single incoming HTTP request just to validate the user's session ID. This introduces 2 to 8 ms of network round-trip latency, connection pool limits, and a critical single point of failure.

Yav employs <strong class="text-paper font-semibold">tamper-proof cryptographic cookie sessions</strong> signed with HMAC-SHA256 (or encrypted with AES-256-GCM). Validation happens completely in-memory via constant-time comparison, yielding microsecond validation with zero external infrastructure.

HMAC-SHA256 Signing

Payload is signed with a secret master key. Signatures are verified in constant time via <code class="text-paper">subtle::ConstantTimeEq</code>, completely immune to timing side-channel attacks.

cryptoconstant-time
Double-Submit CSRF

Every mutating form is automatically supplied with a cryptographic nonce. The server validates that the cookie nonce and the form payload match byte-for-byte.

protectionautomatic
Zero-Infrastructure Auth

Deploy across 20 global regions on bare metal or edge containers without maintaining a distributed Redis cache. Session state travels safely with the user.

statestateless edge
Hardened Security Headers

Automatic injection of <code class="text-paper">SameSite=Lax</code>, <code class="text-paper">HttpOnly</code>, <code class="text-paper">Secure</code>, strict Content-Security-Policy, and HSTS.

scoreA+ Observatory
2.5Concurrency ModelTokio work-stealing

8 cores, 124,500 req/s. Zero lock contention.

In multi-threaded web applications, performance bottlenecks rarely come from raw computation. They stem from thread synchronization: global mutexes, lock contention on session stores, and cache ping-pong across CPU cores.

Yav's architecture eliminates shared mutable state on the request path entirely. Route trees are immutable. Sessions are cryptographic cookies. Telemetry relies strictly on lock-free hardware atomics.

TOKIO WORK-STEALING THREAD ARCHITECTURE8 Hardware Workers

The fastest code is the code that never runs. Yav moves template work to compile time and leaves the request path with nothing left to decide.
